Introduction
This document provides essential information on the components of the Health & Safety Key Issue to
enable users of ESG Ratings to understand how MSCI Sustainability & Climate’s (MSCI S&C’s) outputs
are determined. Health & Safety is a Key Issue in the Social Pillar of the MSCI ESG Ratings model.
Companies are evaluated on their management of workplace safety and the workplace safety standards
in the industries and regions in which they operate.
For additional details on the MSCI ESG Ratings Model, refer to the Data, ratings and scores section of
“ESG Ratings Methodology.”

Risks associated with this Key Issue
• Decreased operational efficiency, production disruptions.
• Increased costs from litigation, penalties and fines.
• Loss of access to markets or growth opportunities from negative reputational effects.
Health & Safety Key Issue score
The Health & Safety Key Issue score evaluates the company’s level of exposure to, and management of,
risks on this Key Issue. The Key Issue score is based on the Exposure score and the Management score
using the formula below. The Exposure score and the Management score are combined such that a
higher level of exposure requires a higher level of demonstrated management capability in order to
achieve the same overall Key Issue score.
𝐾𝐼 = 7 − (max⁡(𝐸𝑋𝑃 ,2) − 𝑀𝐺𝑀𝑇 )
Where:
• 𝐾𝐼 is the Key Issue score for company 𝑖.
• 𝐸𝑋𝑃 is the Exposure score for company 𝑖.
• 𝑀𝐺𝑀𝑇 ⁡is the Management score for company 𝑖.

Health & Safety Management score

modified by controversies.
This score is derived from indicators that are scored on a 0-10 scale, with 10 corresponding to best
practice. Refer to the Analyzing risk management section of “ESG Ratings Methodology” for additional

The definitions of the data points in each component are given below:
Health & Safety Governance & Strategy score
The Health & Safety Governance & Strategy score evaluates the company’s initiatives to manage health
and safety through governance structures, certifications, and comprehensive policy implementation.
Highest initiatives reflect strong leadership accountability, certified management systems, regular audits,
and consistent coverage of employees and contractors. It is expressed as a 0–10 score, where 10
indicates strong initiatives.
• Scope of health and safety policy
Definition: Indicates whether the company’s health and safety policy applies to all operations or select
operations.

• Applicability of health and safety policy to contractors
Definition: Indicates whether contractors are held to the same health and safety policies as employees.
• Health and safety policy and practices are audited
Definition: Indicates whether there is evidence that the company conducts internal and/or external
audits of its health & safety policy and practices. This could include, for example, certification to ISO
45001 or a similar framework, which requires regular audits.
• Health and safety performance is a factor in CEO compensation
Definition: Indicates whether CEO compensation is linked to health and safety performance.
• Body responsible for health & safety strategy and performance
Definition: Assesses whether the health & safety strategy and performance oversight is assigned to a
dedicated individual, team, or committee. Expressed as a 0-10 score, with 10 indicating that the CEO is
responsible for these practices.
o CEO is responsible for health and safety strategy
Definition: Indicates whether the company’s CEO has explicit responsibility for oversight of the
company’s health and safety strategy and performance.
o Senior executive or executive committee are responsible for health and safety
strategy.
Definition: Indicates whether there is a senior executive or executive committee with explicit
responsibility for oversight of the company’s health and safety strategy and performance.
o CSR or sustainability committees are responsible for health and safety strategy and
performance
Definition: Indicates whether there is a CSR or sustainability committee with explicit
responsibility for oversight of the company’s health and safety strategy and performance.
o Non-executive or non-committee level task force is responsible for health and safety
strategy and performance

Definition: Indicates whether there is a non-executive person or non-committee with explicit
responsibility for oversight of the company’s health and safety strategy and performance. An
example of this would be a non-executive risk officer that is responsible for these practices.
• Evaluation of health & safety certification
Definition: Assesses the extent to which the company has obtained recognized health and safety
certifications (e.g., ISO 45001). Expressed as a 0-10 score, with 10 indicating the highest degree of
certification.
o Evidence of health and safety management system certified to recognized standard
Definition: Indicates whether there is evidence that some portion of the company’s operations
have a health and safety management system certified to the ISO 45001 standard, or GB/T
45001-2020 standard.
o Percentage of operations having health and safety management systems certified to
recognized standard
Definition: The percentage of operations that have a health and safety management system
certified to the ISO 45001, or GB/T 45001 -2020 standard.
• Contractors included in disclosed health and safety metrics
Definition: Indicates whether contractor health and safety performance is measured and disclosed in the
same or similar manner as employees.
Health & Safety Targets score
The Health & Safety Targets score evaluates the company’s initiatives to set targets for improving health
and safety performance, including accident and fatality reduction goals that cover both employees and
contractors. Highest initiatives reflect quantifiable, non-zero reduction targets with clear accountability. It
is expressed as a 0–10 score, where 10 indicates strong initiatives.
• Target to improve health and safety performance
Definition: The type of target set by the company to reduce employee accidents and fatalities. Best
practice is to set a quantifiable (non-zero) accident reduction target that includes contractors and
employees.

Health & Safety Performance score
The Health & Safety Performance score evaluates the company’s performance on health and safety
metrics (including lost time incident rate, total recordable injury rate, and fatalities), relative to its peers. It
is expressed as a 0-10 score, where 10 indicates the highest level of performance.
The following provides a non-exhaustive overview of the data points used in the assessment of the
Health & Safety Performance score.
• Lost time incident rate performance relative to peers
Definition: Assesses the company’s performance on reported lost time incidents rate [LTIR] (per million
hours worked), and trend in LTIR, relative to its peers. Expressed as a 0–10 score, where 10 indicates the
highest level of performance.
o Lost time incident rate (per million hours worked) industry relative score
Definition: Assesses the company’s performance on Lost Time Incident Rate (number of incidents
resulting in lost work time per million hours worked) relative to its industry peers. Expressed as a
0–10 score, where 10 indicates strong performance.
▪ Three-year average Lost time incident rate (per million hours worked)
Definition: Measures the company’s three-year average Lost Time Incident Rate (per
million hours worked).
o Lost time incident rate (per million hours worked) industry relative trend score
Definition: Assesses the company’s performance on the three-year average of year-over-year
Lost Time Incident Rate (per million hours worked) trend, relative to its industry peers. Expressed
as a 0–10 score, where 10 indicates strong performance.
▪ Three-year average Lost time incident rate trend (per million hours worked)
Definition: Measures the company’s three-year average of year-over-year Lost Time
Incident Rate (per million hours worked) trend.
• Total recordable injury rate performance relative to peers
Definition: Assesses the company’s performance on reported total recordable injury rate [TRIR] (per
million hours worked), and trend in TRIR, relative to its peers. Expressed as a 0–10 score, where 10
indicates the highest level of performance.
o Total recordable injury rate (per million hours worked) industry relative score
Definition: Assesses the company’s performance on Total Recordable Injury Rate (number of
recordable injuries per million hours worked), relative to its industry peers. Expressed as a 0–10
score, where 10 indicates strong performance.

▪ Three-year average Total recordable injury rate (per million hours worked)
Definition: Measures the company’s three-year average Total Recordable Injury Rate
(per million hours worked).
o Total recordable injury rate (per million hours worked) industry relative trend score
Definition: Assesses the company’s performance on the three-year average of year-over-year
Total Recordable Injury Rate (per million hours worked) trend, relative to its industry peers.
Expressed as a 0–10 score, where 10 indicates strong performance.
▪ Three-year average Total recordable injury rate trend (per million hours
worked)
Definition: Measures the company’s three-year average of year-over-year Total
recordable injury rate (per million hours worked) trend.
• Fatality intensity performance relative to peers
Definition: Assesses the company's performance on fatalities intensity (normalized by number of
employees and/or by sales), relative to industry peers. Expressed as a 0-10 score, with 10 indicating zero
fatalities.
o Fatalities industry relative score
Definition: Assesses the company’s performance on fatalities normalized per 100,000
employees and/or sales, relative to its industry peers. Expressed as a 0–10 score, where 10
indicates strong performance.
▪ Three-year average fatalities (per 100,000 employees)
Definition: Measures the company’s three-year average fatalities per 100,000
employees.
▪ Three-year average fatalities per million USD in sales
Definition: Measures the company’s three-year average fatalities per million USD in
sales.
Controversies
A controversy deduction ranging from 0 to 5 points is subtracted from the overall Management score
based on the severity, status, and the company’s role in the controversies facing the company on this
Key Issue. The result is the Management score. The following categories of controversies are used in the
assessment:
• Health and safety controversies.

For more details on how controversies are included in the MSCI ESG Ratings model, refer to the
Controversies cases section of “ESG Ratings Methodology.”
Health & Safety Exposure score
The Health & Safety Exposure score evaluates the company’s exposure to risks on this Key Issue. It is
based on the Business and Geographic Exposure scores. The Geographic Exposure score functions as a
multiplier on the Business Exposure score, with an impact ranging from -50% to +50%. The Business
and Geographic Exposure scores are scored on a 0-10 scale, with 10 corresponding to the highest risk
and 0 corresponding to the lowest risk. Refer to the Analyzing risk exposure section of “ESG Ratings
Methodology” for additional details. The following formula is used in the Exposure score calculation:
𝐸𝑋𝑃 = 𝐵𝑈𝑆 (1 + 0.1(𝐺𝐸𝑂 − 5))
Where:
• 𝐸𝑋𝑃 is the Health & Safety Exposure score of company 𝑖.
• 𝐵𝑈𝑆 is the Business Exposure score of company 𝑖.
• 𝐺𝐸𝑂 is the Geographic Exposure score of company 𝑖.

The Business Exposure score is a weighted average of the Business Segment Exposure scores of a
company’s business segments. scores are weighted by the proportion of a company’s total assets in
each business segment, using the following formula to calculate the Business Exposure score:

• 𝑛 is the number of business segments of company 𝑖.
Business Segment Exposure scores
The Business Segment Exposure score of a business segment is based on a mapping of the business
segment as disclosed by the company to a corresponding business activity. MSCI S&C uses the
Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) system along with industry-specific adjustments to define
business activities. The score associated with a business activity is used to calculate a Business
Segment Exposure score. Each business activity score is determined by a simple average of the
Accident Rate score of the segment and the Fatality Rate score of the segment:

Where:
• 𝐵𝑆𝐸 is the Business Exposure score for business segment 𝑗.
• 𝐴𝑅 is the Accident Rate score for business activity 𝑗.
• 𝐹𝑅 is the Fatality Rate score for business activity 𝑗.
The Accident Rate score of a business activity is the average of accident rates reported in the United
States by the Occupational Safety & Health Administration (OSHA) and accident rates reported in the
United Kingdom under the Reporting of Injuries, Diseases and Dangerous Occurrences Regulations
(RIDDOR) at a business activity level.

The Fatality Rate score of a business activity is the average of fatality rates reported in the United States
by OSHA and fatality rates reported in the United Kingdom by RIDDOR at a business activity level.
Geographic Exposure score
The Geographic Exposure score is a weighted average of the Exposure scores of the countries, markets
and regions in which a company operates. Scores are weighted by the proportion of a company’s total
assets in each geographic segment through the following equation:
𝐺𝐸𝑂 =⁡∑ 𝑤 𝐺𝑆𝐸
Where:
• 𝐺𝑆𝐸 is the Geographic Segment Exposure score in region 𝑟.
• 𝑤 is the weight of total assets in region 𝑟 for company 𝑖.
• 𝑛 is the number of geographic segments for company 𝑖.
For geographic segments reported as regions (example: Asia Pacific), a nominal GDP-weighted country
or market aggregation is used to calculate region-level scores, using the following equation:
𝐺𝑆𝐸 =⁡∑ 𝑤 𝐺𝐸
Where:
• 𝐺𝑆𝐸 is the Geographic Segment Exposure score of country or market 𝑐.
• 𝑤 is the specific weight of country or market 𝑐 within region 𝑟.

Data sources
The following sources are used to determine the Health & Safety Exposure score:
OSHA, RIDDOR, Bureau of Labor Statistics, ILO, Refinitiv, MSCI S&C, company disclosures.
